pl-l4d42c5-d1e115.summary: Asks whether one may marry his wife's co-mother after the wife's death.

pl-l4d42c5-d1e118.summary: Cites Pope Nicholas, asked whether one may have two co-mothers, one after the other: since man and woman become one flesh, the man becomes co-father to the woman whose co-mother his wife was, so he cannot marry her.
claims: Through one flesh, the husband shares his wife's spiritual kinship.

pl-l4d42c5-d1e127.summary: Cites a contrary text: one who has a spiritual co-father, whose son he received from the font, while his wife is not co-mother, may marry the co-father's widow after his death, since no spiritual generation separates them.

pl-l4d42c5-d1e134.summary: Cites Paschal: after the wife's death, no reason or authority seems to forbid marrying the wife's co-mother, since one does not pass through carnal union to spiritual union.
claims: Spiritual kinship does not pass through carnal union.

pl-l4d42c5-d1e146.summary: Reconciles: Nicholas concerns one who rendered the debt to his wife after she became co-mother; the others concern one whose wife became co-mother after he left her and was not known by him after, or rather one whose wife died before he knew her.
claims: Intercourse after the co-parenthood transmits the impediment.

pl-l4d42c5.summary: Asks whether one may marry his late wife's co-mother. Nicholas forbids it, since husband and wife become one flesh, so the husband becomes co-father to his wife's co-mother. Others allow it, as Paschal says no reason forbids it, since spiritual union does not pass through carnal union. Lombard reconciles: Nicholas concerns a man who had intercourse with his wife after she became co-mother; the others, one whose wife became co-mother after he left her and was not known by him afterward, or who died before he knew her.
claims: Whether one may marry a late wife's co-mother is disputed.
Spiritual kinship passes to the husband through intercourse after the co-parenthood.
